## Overview

`cyclotraj` tests whether treatment groups differ in how repeatedly-measured
units change over time, when each observation is a count out of a
sample-specific total. Counts are modeled with binomial generalized linear
mixed-effects models (logit link), in two parameterizations of time that are
read together:

* a **continuous-time** (linear-slope) model, for each treatment's overall rate
  of expansion or contraction, and
* a **difference-in-differences** (categorical-time) model, for
  timepoint-specific treatment effects with no linearity assumption.

Random intercepts for unit and subject absorb the nested, repeated-measures
structure. The package replaces marginal Wilcoxon testing with model-based
inference, and nothing in it is domain specific: any nested longitudinal count
data has this structure. The function and argument names keep the vocabulary of
the motivating application, where the repeated-measures unit is a T-cell clone
(`clone`) and the subject it is nested in is a patient (`patient`).

The example data used throughout this vignette are **synthetic**, simulated
from the model above by `data-raw/make_example_data.R`. Six trajectory groups
are generated with deliberately different shapes, so the two time encodings
agree in some groups and disagree in others.

## Workflow

```{r setup}
library(cyclotraj)
```

### 1. Prepare the data

`prepare_clone_data()` validates and standardizes a long-format table. Column
names are mapped through arguments, so data with any column naming works.

```{r prep}
raw <- read_example_data()          # bundled synthetic example
d <- prepare_clone_data(raw, treatment_ref = "arm_A")
levels(d$treatment)                 # reference arm first
table(d$trajectory)
```

### 2. Run the analysis

`run_clone_analysis()` fits both models to every trajectory and computes the
inference and diagnostics.

```{r run, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
res <- run_clone_analysis(raw, treatment_ref = "arm_A")
res
```

`results_table()` collates the joint Wald tests (does each treatment alter each
trajectory at all?):

```{r results}
head(results_table(res), 8)
```

### 3. Inspect one trajectory

Trajectory 5 is simulated with a sustained `arm_D` slope effect, so both time
encodings should find it.

```{r one}
tr <- res$trajectories[["Traj 5"]]
tr$joint_wald$continuous
subset(tr$slopes, select = c("contrast", "estimate", "p.value"))
```

### 4. When the two time encodings disagree

Trajectory 3 gives `arm_D` a transient one-timepoint spike at week 3 instead of
a sustained trend. A single slope has to average that spike over the whole
follow-up, so the continuous-time omnibus test barely clears the conventional
threshold, while the difference-in-differences test, which is free to place the
effect at one timepoint, is emphatic. Reading the two together is what locates
the effect in time.

```{r disagree}
rt <- results_table(res)
rt[rt$trajectory == "Traj 3" & rt$treatment == "arm_D", ]
```

The post-hoc contrasts say where it sits. Of the six interval contrasts
comparing `arm_A` with `arm_D`, the three that involve week 3 are the
significant ones and the three that do not are nowhere near significance, which
is the signature of a one-timepoint spike rather than a trend. Estimates are on
the log odds ratio scale.

```{r disagree-posthoc}
dc <- res$trajectories[["Traj 3"]]$did_contrasts
dc <- dc[dc$treatments == "arm_A - arm_D", c("timepoints", "estimate", "p.value")]
dc[order(dc$p.value), ]
```

### 5. Plot with confidence bands

```{r plot, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
sub <- d[d$trajectory == "Traj 5", ]
plot_trajectory(sub, tr$continuous, title = "Traj 5: continuous-time fit")
```

## Using your own data

Map your columns and (optionally) omit the trajectory argument to treat the data
as a single group:

```{r generic, eval = FALSE}
res <- run_clone_analysis(
  my_data,
  clone = "lineage_id", patient = "subject", treatment = "arm",
  timepoint = "week", count = "reads", total = "library_size",
  trajectory = NULL, treatment_ref = "control"
)
```
